extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of political theory and comparative government; policymakers interested in democratic institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for judging the qualities, costs, and foreign-policy capacity of democratic governments (comparative observations chiefly about the United States and France). Useful for assessing taxation burden, corruption, public economy, civic self-control, military mobilization, and foreign policy prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute actual amount of taxation (direct and indirect)
rubrics_metrics.description: I confine myself to a computation of the actual amount of taxation, without investigating the relation which subsists between the taxation and the revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the sum total of direct and indirect taxes levied on citizens. Note practical obstacles: central administrations may have data but not publish it; local/communal expenses are often uncomputed or inaccessible (example: difficulty obtaining county and township budgets in the United States). Use available county budgets (e.g., Pennsylvania counties) cautiously because incomplete years/parts yield only partial estimates. Beware that an apparently exact per-capita figure may apply only to a limited set of objects or years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for structural differences before comparing national budgets
rubrics_metrics.description: No fair comparison can be instituted between [French and American budgets]... the elements of which they are composed always differ more or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing expenditures across nations, account for differences in which objects are included in central vs. subcentral budgets (e.g., Union vs. French central government), municipal responsibilities, and the organization of local bodies (New England vs. Georgia vs. Pennsylvania vs. Illinois). Specific differences to adjust for: state payment of clergy (France) vs. voluntary religion (U.S.); legal provision for the poor; public officer salaries vs. perquisites; use of contributions in kind vs. turnpikes/road tolls; standing army and navy sizes. Failure to control for these structural differences invalidates direct budget comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the false affectation of exactness in statistical comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: When statistics are not based upon computations which are strictly accurate, they mislead instead of guiding aright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandon or suspend numerical investigation rather than publish numerics based on incomplete or non-analogous data. The mind is easily imposed upon by falsely precise figures; prefer qualitative signs if quantitative comparability is not attainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use external social indicators to judge taxation relative to prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of positive documents, we may form an opinion as to the proportion which the taxation of a people bears to its real prosperity, by observing whether its external appearance is flourishing; whether, after having discharged the calls of the State, the poor man retains the means of subsistence, and the rich the means of enjoyment; and whether both classes are contented with their position, seeking, however, to ameliorate it by perpetual exertions, so that industry is never in want of capital, nor capital unemployed by industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When exact fiscal data are unavailable or not comparable, evaluate whether ordinary life remains comfortable post-taxation: subsistence for poor, enjoyment for rich, contentment and productive circulation of capital. These qualitative signs can indicate whether citizens contribute a burdensome portion of income to the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local political organization constrains data collection and comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority of the Federal government cannot oblige the provincial governments to throw any light upon this point; and even if these governments were inclined to afford their simultaneous co-operation, it may be doubted whether they possess the means of procuring a satisfactory answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that federal systems with autonomous local officers (e.g., county and town magistrates not appointed by state authorities) hinder centralized data collection. Anticipate non-cooperation or incapability of subordinate officers to supply reliable returns; this limits the accuracy of national per-capita taxation estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether democratic government is ‘cheap’ (economy of government)
rubrics_metrics.description: I conclude ... that the democratic government of the Americans is not a cheap government, as is sometimes asserted; and I have no hesitation in predicting that ... its taxation will speedily be increased to the rate of that which prevails in the greater part of the aristocracies and the monarchies of Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate expenditures driven by democratic politics: expenditures to satisfy lower orders (poor relief, public instruction), liberal pay for many services, generous remuneration of subordinate agents, and efforts to open power to many. These tendencies tend to increase public spending. Use evidence of sustained public programs and patronage to gauge costliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corruption profile: susceptibility differs by regime and affects public morality
rubrics_metrics.description: In aristocracies rulers sometimes endeavor to corrupt the people—In democracies rulers frequently show themselves to be corrupt—In the former their vices are directly prejudicial to the morality of the people—In the latter their indirect influence is still more pernicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating corruption risk and its social effect, consider rulers' socioeconomic origins: aristocratic rulers are often wealthy and less driven by money, while democratic leaders often seek to make fortunes and may be more open to corrupt inducements. In democracies, rulers' corrupt conduct lends official sanction to base practices, making corruption contagious and more damaging to public morality than isolated aristocratic vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political example effect: rapid social contagion from rulers' rise
rubrics_metrics.description: In a democracy private citizens see a man of their own rank in life, who rises from that obscure position, and who becomes possessed of riches and of power in a few years; the spectacle excites their surprise and their envy ... they are led ... to impute his success mainly to some one of his defects; and an odious mixture is thus formed of the ideas of turpitude and power, unworthiness and success, utility and dishonor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether upward mobility of public figures is attributed to corrupt means rather than talent; when the populace perceives rapid enrichment/power as possibly linked to dishonorable conduct, that perception encourages imitation and weakens public virtue. Use anecdotes about public appointments, scandals, and popular explanations of success as indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for sustained national effort under democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy appears to me to be much better adapted for the peaceful conduct of society, or for an occasional effort of remarkable vigor, than for the hardy and prolonged endurance of the storms which beset the political existence of nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a democracy's ability to sustain long-term mobilization by: presence or absence of compulsory enlistment/conscription or impressment; willingness of the populace to undergo privations over time; institutional mechanisms that enforce taxation and recruitment; and cultural disposition toward long-term calculation versus immediate feeling. Democracies often show initial enthusiasm but difficulty maintaining prolonged sacrifices; reliance on voluntary enlistment and bounties (rather than conscription) implies limits for protracted continental or maritime wars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-control and legislative acquiescence in democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: The difficulty which a democracy has in conquering the passions and in subduing the exigencies of the moment, with a view to the future, is conspicuous ... The American people acquiesces slowly, or frequently does not acquiesce, in what is beneficial to its interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating democratic lawmaking and compliance: note that legislation is made by and for the people and thus often reflects popular immediate interests rather than long-term public good. Examples: tolerance of fraudulent bankruptcies because of widespread bankruptcies; political resistance to duties (e.g., on brandy) for fear of losing votes. Still, democracies can correct errors via experience if the populace attains sufficient education and civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-policy maxims for prudence (Washington/Jefferson principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: The great rule of conduct for us in regard to foreign nations is, in extending our commercial relations, to have with them as little political connection as possible... It is our true policy to steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world ... honesty is always the best policy ... Taking care always to keep ourselves, by suitable establishments, in a respectable defensive posture, we may safely trust to temporary alliances for extraordinary emergencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate foreign-policy choices by these standards: prioritize commercial relations over political entanglement; observe existing engagements in good faith but avoid extending permanent alliances; refrain from soliciting foreign privileges (Jefferson's maxim); maintain sufficient defensive preparedness so neutrality can be respected. Use historical adherence to these maxims as a measure of prudent policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign affairs require qualities democracies often lack
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign politics demand scarcely any of those qualities which a democracy possesses; and they require, on the contrary, the perfect use of almost all those faculties in which it is deficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a democracy's fitness for managing external relations, test for presence of: practical discretion born of experience, capacity to regulate details of important undertakings, perseverance in designs despite obstacles, secrecy in combining measures, and patience to await consequences. If these faculties are weak, the state may be inferior in foreign policy compared with aristocratic or monarchical governments.
